blocks.text: The SFT training pipeline is the concrete sequence of steps that turns a fully prepared dataset into an actual trained model, choosing hyperparameters, launching the run, monitoring it as it progresses, checkpointing along the way, and knowing when to stop.
This topic closes out the Supervised Fine-Tuning module by tying together the dataset preparation work from earlier modules with the practical mechanics of actually running a training job.
1. From Prepared Dataset to a Trained Model

blocks.alt: A prepared dataset goes through a training run to become a trained model

blocks.text: By the time a dataset reaches this stage, it has already passed through collection, cleaning, formatting, and tokenization, all covered in earlier modules, the training pipeline is what actually consumes that prepared data and produces a fine-tuned model as output.
2. Choosing Hyperparameters for an SFT Run

blocks.alt: Learning rate, batch size, and epochs together define the training configuration

blocks.text: The core hyperparameters, learning rate, how large each weight update step is, batch size, how many examples are processed together per step, and epochs, how many full passes through the dataset training runs for, together shape how training unfolds, a topic covered in far more depth in the Training Fundamentals module immediately following this one.
3. Monitoring Loss During Training

blocks.alt: Each training step produces a loss value, which together form a loss curve

blocks.text: Watching the loss curve, the training loss value plotted over the course of training, is the most basic and immediate signal available for whether training is progressing normally, a steadily decreasing curve is generally a healthy sign, while a flat or erratic curve often signals a problem worth investigating.
4. Checkpointing Throughout an SFT Run

blocks.alt: Training progress produces checkpoint one, checkpoint two, and checkpoint three along the way

blocks.text: Rather than only saving the final model at the very end of training, saving intermediate checkpoints at regular intervals lets you compare model quality at different points in training, and recover a good earlier state if later training somehow degrades quality rather than improving it.

blocks.title: Checkpoints also protect against infrastructure failures
blocks.content: Regular checkpointing means a training job interrupted by a hardware failure or timeout, a real concern covered in the Training Infrastructure module later in this course, does not lose all progress made before the interruption.

blocks.text: 5. Early Stopping Based on Validation Loss

blocks.alt: Rising validation loss triggers stopping training early

blocks.text: Tracking loss on a held out validation set, separate from the training data itself, reveals when a model has stopped genuinely improving and started overfitting, memorizing training specific patterns rather than learning generalizable behavior, typically visible as training loss continuing to fall while validation loss starts rising.

blocks.text: 6. Common SFT Training Failures

blocks.alt: Loss not decreasing and loss exploding are both common causes worth investigating

blocks.text: Loss that never meaningfully decreases often points to a learning rate set too low, a bug in the label masking covered in the earlier Tokenization Pipeline topic, or a dataset with inconsistent or contradictory examples confusing the training signal.
Loss that explodes or turns into NaN values typically points to a learning rate set too high, or a rare malformed example slipping through cleaning and destabilizing a specific training step.
7. From Training Complete to Evaluation

blocks.alt: Training complete leads directly into held out evaluation

blocks.text: A finished training run is not the end of the fine-tuning workflow covered in the Introduction module, it hands off directly to evaluation, testing the resulting model against a genuinely held out set of examples, covered in full depth in this course dedicated Evaluation module.
8. A Minimal SFT Pipeline Script

A minimal end to end SFT pipeline loads the prepared dataset, initializes the pretrained base model, configures the chosen hyperparameters, runs the training loop with periodic checkpointing and validation loss tracking, and saves the final model, the same basic shape regardless of which specific framework, covered in the Fine-Tuning Frameworks module, actually implements it.
9. Iterating on the Pipeline Based on Results

A first SFT run rarely produces the final model. Results from evaluation typically point back to specific improvements, more data for an underrepresented case, a hyperparameter adjustment, or a dataset quality issue, closing the loop back to the iterative fine-tuning workflow introduced early in this course.
Worked Example

A team runs their first SFT training pass on a prepared support reply dataset, watching the loss curve steadily decrease over the first epoch before flattening out during the second, while validation loss starts creeping upward partway through the third epoch.

Rather than running the full three planned epochs, they load the checkpoint saved just before validation loss started rising, avoiding the overfit later checkpoints, and move that earlier checkpoint forward into evaluation, where it performs noticeably better than the final epoch checkpoint would have.
Common Mistakes

items: Only saving the final model checkpoint, with no way to recover a better performing earlier state
Ignoring validation loss entirely and judging training success purely by training loss alone
Not investigating an unusual loss curve, assuming it will resolve itself as training continues
Treating a completed training run as the end of the process rather than the start of evaluation and iteration

Key Takeaway

The SFT training pipeline turns a prepared dataset into a trained model through careful hyperparameter choice, active loss monitoring, regular checkpointing, and validation based early stopping, and treating a completed run as the start of evaluation and iteration, rather than the finish line, is what actually produces a genuinely improved fine-tuned model over successive rounds.
